title: Lynx: Symmetric Primitive for Shorter and Faster VOLE-in-the-Head Signatures
authors: Lin Jiao, Hongsen Yang, Hongrui Cui, Yituo He, Yonglin Hao, Xiaojie Guo, Qunxiong Zheng, Jiang Zhang, Yu Yu, and Kang Yang
abstract: VOLE-in-the-Head (VOLEitH) is one of the most promising frameworks to design post-quantum digital signatures based on symmetric primitives. However, all existing symmetric primitives do not capture the specialized characteristics of the VOLEitH framework and are not VOLEitH-friendly, leaving room for improving the efficiency of VOLEitH-based signatures. In this paper, we propose a VOLEitH-friendly symmetric primitive called Lynx, which is optimal in terms of the number of required VOLE correlations that directly determines the efficiency of VOLEitH-based signature schemes. In particular, Lynx adopts a multi-branch structure featuring a new truncation function: (a) nonlinear components are customized to minimize the witness length and polynomial degree, as well as the number of finite-field multiplications; (b) linear layers are strategically interleaved to strengthen security. The security of Lynx is rigorously validated by covering all possible attacks in the presence of both classical and quantum adversaries. Built upon Lynx, we design a post-quantum signature scheme, Lynxer, in the VOLEitH framework, which is shorter and faster than all known post-quantum signature schemes from symmetric primitives. According to our experimental results, compared to the state-of-the-art symmetric-based signature schemes in the same setting, i.e., Rainier (CCS’22), AIMer (CCS’23) and FAESTv2 (Crypto’25), our signature scheme Lynxer reduces the “public-key size + signature size” by 25% ∼ 51%, and improves the signing (resp., verification) time up to 90.6% (resp., 89.3%).

1      Introduction
Digital signatures constitute the most fundamental primitive in cryptography. It is well-
known that the widely deployed RSA-based and discrete-logarithm-based signature schemes
are insecure when large-scale quantum computers become a reality [Sho94]. To address
this security threat, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) called
for submissions of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) algorithms in 2016. For now,
NIST has standardized two post-quantum signature schemes (i.e., ML-DSA [NIS24a] and
SLH-DSA [NIS24b]), and is finalizing a third (i.e., Falcon [FHK+ 21]). To broaden the
design diversity and hardness assumptions, NIST has issued a new call for additional
post-quantum signature candidates [NIS22], currently in the second round.

     Symmetric-based signature schemes (i.e., those based only on symmetric primitives)
are among the most promising post-quantum signature schemes. The MPC-in-the-Head
(MPCitH) framework [IKOS07] is a key paradigm for designing symmetric-based signature
schemes. In such signature schemes, a pair of public and secret keys consists of y = f (x) and
x, where f is a One-Way Function (OWF); a signature is a non-interactive zero-knowledge
(NIZK) proof of knowledge of secret key x, generated by locally emulating an MPC
protocol execution in the head and applying the cut-and-choose technique for soundness.
Picnic [ZCD+ 17], built on [GMO16, CDG+ 17, KKW18], is the first post-quantum signature
scheme based on symmetric primitives and MPCitH in NIST’s PQC standardization process
and a third-round alternate candidate of the NIST PQC competition. It uses an MPC-
friendly block cipher LowMC [ARS+ 15] to reduce the number of AND gates and thus
the size of signatures. Subsequent works such as Banquet [BDK+ 21] and Limbo [DOT21]
improved the efficiency of Picnic by replacing LowMC with AES.
     While LowMC is a block cipher, it is overkill for MPCitH-based signature schemes that
only require an OWF. Initially, Dobraunig et al. [DKR+ 22] proposed a tailor-made MPCitH-
friendly OWF (named RAIN), and used it to design a symmetric-based post-quantum
signature scheme Rainier in the Picnic framework. Later, Kim et al. [KHS+ 23] designed
an alternative MPCitH-friendly OWF (named AIM) and combined it with an improved
Picnic framework BN++ [KZ22] to obtain the symmetric-based signature scheme AIMer.
Specifically, AIMer has been selected as a finalist in Korea’s PQC competition [Kpq26]. Due
to the cryptanalysis [ZWY+ 23, LMØM23] that weakened its security, AIM was upgraded
to AIM2 to resist those attacks [KHSL23]. Design-wise, RAIN uses full-state large-field
inversion S-boxes, whereas AIM2 adopts Mersenne-exponent power-map S-boxes.
     Recently, the VOLE-in-the-Head (VOLEitH) framework [BBD+ 23b] was introduced to
design symmetric-based post-quantum signature schemes. VOLEitH can be viewed as a
fundamental improvement over MPCitH [BBM+ 24, FR25]; it locally emulates a Vector
Oblivious Linear Evaluation (VOLE) protocol [Roy22] execution in the head, and then uses
a VOLE-based zero-knowledge proof (e.g., QuickSilver [YSWW21]) to prove knowledge
of the secret key. Using AES to instantiate an OWF, Baum et al. [BBD+ 23b] designed
a VOLEitH-based post-quantum signature scheme FAEST, and FAEST achieves shorter
signature size and faster signing/verification time than MPCitH-based signature schemes
from AES. The first version of FAEST (i.e., FAESTv1) was submitted to the NIST PQC
competition for additional digital signature schemes [BBD+ 23a]. Subsequently, FAESTv1
was improved in [BBM+ 24, BBB+ 25], resulting in FAESTv2 [BBB+ 24], which has advanced
to the second round of the competition. However, compared to the symmetric-based
signature schemes from MPCitH-friendly OWFs [DKR+ 22, KHS+ 23], the most optimized
version of FAEST (i.e., FAESTv2), based on AES, still requires a larger communication cost
(i.e., “public-key size + signature size”1 ). This motivates us to design VOLEitH-friendly
symmetric primitives.
     However, no tailored symmetric primitive has been designed to capture the special-
ized characteristics of the VOLEitH framework. Specifically, the primary design goal
of existing MPCitH-friendly symmetric primitives [DKR+ 22, KHS+ 23] is to reduce the
number of multiplication gates, since MPCitH compiles an OWF into a circuit, and
fewer multiplication gates enable shorter signature sizes and faster computation times.
Nevertheless, the VOLEitH framework encodes an OWF as a polynomial over a finite
field, and the polynomial degree and witness length dominate the signature size and
computation time of signature schemes in this framework. Therefore, RAIN [DKR+ 22] and
AIM2 [KHSL23] are not VOLE-friendly. Furthermore, to prove security in the Quantum
Random Oracle Model (QROM), the VOLEitH-based signature scheme FAESTv2 assumes
that the underlying function f behind public and private keys is not only one-way but
also satisfies a special pseudorandomness property (i.e., f (x) is computationally indistin-

    In the pre-quantum era, symmetric primitives often support 128-bit, 192-bit, and
256-bit security against classical attacks. Accordingly, in the post-quantum era, they are
expected to support 128-bit, 192-bit, and 256-bit security in the presence of quantum
attacks, corresponding to 256-bit, 384-bit, and 512-bit classical security, respectively,
due to the Grover’s quantum algorithm [Gro96] 2 . Cryptographic algorithms with
classical security beyond 256 bits may be desirable in high-assurance applications (e.g.,
national infrastructure and long-term archives). In particular, both NIST and ISO/IEC
have reserved space for security levels beyond 256 bits [Bar20, ISO24]. Furthermore,
cryptographic hash functions with 384- or 512-bit security levels, such as SHAKE-512 [M2̈5]
with 512-bit security, have already been developed. In the recent PQC competition [Ins25],
for both public-key and private-key cryptographic algorithms, supporting a 512-bit security
level is required and providing a 384-bit security level is encouraged. However, to date,
there are no symmetric-based signature schemes that support 384-bit or 512-bit security
levels. This motivates us to design a post-quantum signature scheme from a VOLEitH-
friendly symmetric primitive, which supports all five security levels (i.e., 128, 192, 256, 384
and 512 bits).


1.1     Our Contributions
In this paper, we propose Lynx, a tailored VOLEitH-friendly symmetric primitive supporting
all five security levels (128, 192, 256, 384, and 512 bits). It features a multi-branch structure
centered on a finite-field-multiplication-based truncation function, as well as customized
nonlinear components and interleaved linear layers. This design simultaneously minimizes
the crucial metrics that determine the “pk + sig” size, i.e., the witness length and the
degree of constraint polynomials (i.e., those proven in zero-knowledge). Moreover, while
prioritizing optimal communication cost, Lynx also minimizes the number of finite field
multiplications within the constraint polynomials at each security level, which is a notable
factor governing signing and verification latency (see Section 1.2 for technical details).
Since the attack model limits adversaries to accessing only a single input-output pair,
our analysis comprehensively evaluates Lynx against advanced algebraic attacks targeting
key recovery, as cited in [YZY+ 24, YZY25, ZWY+ 23, SS21, CKPS00, Din21, LMØM23,
LMM24a, SCL+ 25]. Furthermore, it extends to an assessment of pseudorandomness,
incorporating statistical distinguishers and standardized randomness tests to validate
the QROM security proof in FAESTv2 [BBB+ 24]. We also assess the resilience of Lynx
against quantum attacks, accounting for the quadratic speedup of Grover’s algorithm.
Built on Lynx, we propose Lynxer, a new post-quantum signature scheme in the VOLEitH
framework, and offer a “small” variant for minimal communication cost and a “fast” variant
for low latency at each security level.
     We evaluate the performance of Lynxer using both reference and optimized imple-
mentations. The results show that Lynxer outperforms state-of-the-art symmetric-based
post-quantum signature schemes in both “pk + sig” size and signing/verification run-
time. Lynxer’s minimum “pk + sig” sizes are 2970/6700/12064 bytes at 128/192/256-bit
common security levels. Compared to the optimized VOLEitH-based signature schemes
from standard AES and its EM variant (i.e., FAESTv2 [BBB+ 24]), Lynxer reduces the
“pk + sig” size by 34.6%∼44.2% for FAEST and by 24.6%∼37.0% for FAEST-EM. Com-
pared to the symmetric-based signature schemes from MPCitH-friendly OWFs, the re-
duction is 41.8%∼50.8% for Rianier-3/4 and 26.9%∼41.1% for the updated AIMer (i.e.,

1.2    Technical Overview
This section addresses three core design challenges in Lynx; further details are in Section 3.
Minimizing communication cost. The core focus in QuickSilver-style VOLEitH pro-
tocols is the “pk + sig” size, which is dominated by (i) the witness length ` and (ii)
the degree bound of constraint polynomials d. Our primitive is defined over F2n , where
the parameter n matches the desired security level. It is engineered to jointly minimize
these two parameters, achieving the highly efficient configuration of d = 2 and ` = 3n.
This configuration is minimal under the constraint of resisting the attack described in
[ZWY+ 23], thereby yielding a signature size that scales optimally as 5n + B across all
security levels in the VOLEitH framework, where B is a small constant.
Ensuring robust security. Achieving better communication cost must not compromise
security. Lynx’s structure, especially the nonlinear truncation function, generates cross-
terms among pairwise witness variables in the constraint polynomials. Concurrently, the
linear layers are carefully designed to ensure high-degree terms for every witness variable.
These techniques strengthen resilience against advanced large-field algebraic attacks (e.g.,
resultant and linearized polynomial decomposition attacks [YZY+ 24, YZY25, SCL+ 25]).
Moreover, the linear layers are interleaved with nonlinear components, effectively prevent-
ing the elimination of variables from spawning additional Boolean equations [LMØM23,
LMM24a]. This isolation enhances resistance against F2 -based algebraic attacks (such
as XL, Gröbner Basis Attacks [SS21, CKPS00]). Finally, the use of random linear layers
and constant additions ensures that attacks requiring multiple input-output pairs become
fundamentally inapplicable.
Enabling scalable security levels. To support all five security levels ranging from 128-
bit to 512-bit within a uniform structure, we employ a customized approach for nonlinear
components. In addition to the truncation functions, we use diverse power permutations
(e.g., inverse, Mersenne, and Kasami [Gol68] functions), with their relevant parameters
being (i) the number of multiplications in the constraint polynomial and (ii) the number
of Boolean equations derived from the constraint polynomial. We set different exponent
selections for each security level. This not only tightly controls the overdefined degree of
the Boolean equation system for mitigating the threat posed by XL and Gröbner basis
attacks, but also ensures that the number of finite field multiplications and Frobenius
endomorphisms required in the constraint polynomials is optimized at each security level.
For example, specific candidates such as Kasami mapping and extended truncation function
compress 2 multiplications into a single nonlinear component, generating only a set of
Boolean equations without increasing extra witness. Furthermore, we use these power
permutations and their inverse functions simultaneously to ensure high algebraic degrees
are achieved in both the forward and inverse evaluation directions. Consequently, Lynxer
delivers scalable security across all target levels with optimized performance.

3.3     Cryptanalysis
In VOLEitH-based signatures, each randomly sampled secret k is uniquely bound to a
randomly sampled initial vector iv, and together they produce exactly one output t. Given

resistance; for indistinguishability, it aims to distinguish t from a uniformly random string.
This naturally extends to the multi-user setting, where the adversary is given multiple
independent {(ivi , ti )}i pairs.

and private keys. Furthermore, FN-DSA [PFH+ 22], standardizing in FIPS 206 and derived
from FALCON based on SVP over NTRU lattices, requires complex operations such as
(discrete) Gaussian sampling or complex float/fix point arithmetic.

in FIPS 205 and derived from SPHINCS+ with security rooted in SHA-2 and SHAKE
hash functions, Lynxer-128f reduces the “pk + sig” size by 53.3% relative to their small
variants, while achieving a signing speedup of 403∼480 times at comparable verification
runtime. When compared to their fast variants, Lynxer-128f reduces the “pk + sig” size by
78.5%, signing runtime by a factor of 19∼24 times, and verification runtime by a factor of
2.1∼2.5 times.

symmetric-based signature schemes. Picnic [ZCD+ 20] is the first NIST PQC alternate
candidate built on MPCitH and MPC-friendly block cipher LowMC. The “pk + sig” size
of Picnic-L1-full is 11 times that of Lynx-128s at comparable runtime. The runtime of
Picnic3-L1 is 31∼35 times that of Lynx-128f, and its “pk + sig” size is 4 times. Ban-
quet [BDK+ 21] and Limbo [DOT21] built upon Picnic by replacing LowMC with AES.
Compared to Banquet, Lynxer reduces the “pk + sig” size by over 70% in both variants,
while accelerating signing and verification by about 16 times in small variants and over
110 times in fast variants. Compared to Limbo, Lynxer cuts the “pk + sig” size by over
70%. BN++Rain3/4 [KZ22] adopts an improved Picnic framework (BN++) that slightly
reduces the “pk + sig” size and runtime compared to the earlier Rainier [DKR+ 22], but
the overall reduction ratios compared with Lynxer are not significantly different from those
of Rainier in Table 7.

only Lynxer achieve a “pk + sig” size below 3 KB at 128-bit security level. It also demon-
